blocks.text: When molecules are bombarded with fast electrons they lose an electron, forming a positively charged molecular ion with one unpaired electron: molecule -> molecule.+ + e- (electron bombardment). The molecular ion can break up further into new ions, molecules and free radicals.

Each peak corresponds to an ion of a particular m/e. The peak with the highest m/e is usually the molecular ion (M+) peak, which gives the molecular mass of the compound. In Example 29.4 the molecular ion peak is at m/e 58, so the spectrum belongs to propanal, CH3CH2CHO (Mr 58), not butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO (Mr 72).

blocks.alt: Stick mass spectrum, relative intensity (0 to 100) against m/e (10 to 75). The tallest peaks are at m/e 27, 28 and 29 (about 60, 90 and 99) and at m/e 58 (about 85); small peaks lie near 15, 18, 26, 30, 39, 57 and 59.
blocks.caption: Example 29.4: mass spectrum (original drawing after the spectrum printed with Example 29.4).

blocks.text: Different compounds can have the same molecular mass, so fragmentation helps to find the structure. Fragments appear as smaller characteristic ions or from the loss of small molecules, giving peaks at, for example, 18 (H2O), 29 (C2H5+) and 44 (CO2). Simple alkanes break at their C-C bonds: straight-chain hexane gives peaks at 86 (C6H14+), 71 (C5H11+), 57 (C4H9+), 43 (C3H7+), 29 (C2H5+) and 15 (CH3+).
c) The M+1 and M+2 peaks

The M+1 peak is caused by carbon-13 in the molecule. About 1.1% of all carbon atoms are 13C, so the M+1 peak is much smaller than the M peak, and the more carbon atoms a molecule has, the taller its M+1 peak (hexane's M+1 peak is relatively larger than ethane's). The number of carbon atoms, n, is n = (100 x abundance of M+1) / (1.1 x abundance of M+). In Example 29.5 the M peak at m/e 58 has abundance about 85 and the M+1 peak at 59 has abundance 3, so n = (100 x 3) / (1.1 x 85) = 3.21, that is three carbon atoms.

blocks.alt: Stick mass spectrum of compound X, relative abundance (0 to 100) against m/e (10 to 60). Tall peaks at m/e 43 (about 98) and m/e 58 (about 84), a peak at 15 (about 24), a small peak at 59 (3) and other small peaks.
blocks.caption: Example 29.5: mass spectrum of compound X (original drawing after the spectrum printed with Example 29.5).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed spectrum the M+1 peak at 59 stands a little above 3, while the worked answer uses 3; it is drawn at 3.

Bromine and chlorine atoms give an M+2 (and possibly an M+4) peak. Chlorine exists as 35Cl and 37Cl in a 3:1 ratio, so a compound with one Cl atom shows M and M+2 peaks in the ratio 3:1, and one with two Cl atoms shows M, M+2 and M+4 in the ratio 9:6:1. Bromine exists as 79Br and 81Br in almost equal amounts, so one Br atom gives M and M+2 peaks of equal height (1:1), and two Br atoms give M, M+2 and M+4 in the ratio 1:2:1.

blocks.alt: Four stick spectra of % abundance against m/e. Compounds containing 1 Cl atom: 3 (M+ peak) at 35 and 1 ([M + 2] peak) at 37. Compounds containing 2 Cl atoms: 9 (M+ peak) at 70, 6 ([M + 2] peak) at 72 and 1 ([M + 4] peak) at 74. Compounds containing 1 Br atom: equal peaks, 1 (M+ peak) at 79 and 1 ([M + 2] peak) at 81. Compounds containing 2 Br atoms: 1 (M+ peak) at 158, 2 ([M + 2] peak) at 160 and 1 ([M + 4] peak) at 162.
blocks.caption: M+, [M + 2] and [M + 4] peaks of compounds containing chlorine and bromine atoms (original drawing after the four spectra printed in 29.6.2).
